title: Checking a JSON document
description:
Data from an API should be checked where it enters your program (lesson 1.03). Write the check for a book, and the canonical form you would send back.

```python
def parse_book(text): ...
def to_canonical_json(book): ...
```

**parse_book** takes JSON text and returns a dict with exactly the keys `id`, `title`, `year`, `tags` and `price`. It raises `ValueError` with a message starting with the field's path when anything is wrong:

| Field | Rule | Message starts with |
|---|---|---|
| the text | valid JSON | `book: invalid JSON` |
| the document | an object | `book: expected an object` |
| `id` | required; an integer (not a boolean), at least 1 | `book.id` |
| `title` | required; a string, not empty after stripping spaces; returned stripped | `book.title` |
| `year` | optional; missing or `null` gives `None`; else an integer (not a boolean) | `book.year` |
| `tags` | optional; missing gives `[]`; else a list of strings | `book.tags` |
| `price` | optional; missing or `null` gives `None`; else a number (integer or float, not a boolean), not negative | `book.price` |

Other keys in the document are ignored.

**to_canonical_json** returns the JSON text for a book dict with keys sorted, no spaces (`separators=(",", ":")`) and non-ASCII characters kept as they are, so that the same book always gives exactly the same text.
hints: Check the fields in the order of the table, each with its own `raise`, so the first problem decides the message.
`isinstance(True, int)` is true, so every "integer" check also needs `not isinstance(value, bool)`.
